nameStory: The 'wood' part of wood crane's-bill comes from its Latin name 'sylvaticum,' meaning 'of woodland,' where this European native naturally grows. The 'crane's-bill' name comes from the long, pointed seed pods that look remarkably like a crane's beak - a feature shared by all plants in the geranium family.
description: Wood crane's-bill is a hardy perennial wildflower with deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves and five-petaled flowers that bloom in shades of pink to purple. This European native occasionally escapes cultivation in New England, forming low clumps about 1-2 feet tall. The plant produces the characteristic long, pointed seed pods that give all crane's-bills their memorable name.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five rounded petals in pink to purple shades, about an inch across, with distinct darker veins running through each petal like tiny roadmaps

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided into 5-7 finger-like segments, feeling soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, arranged alternately along the stem

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, pointed seed pods resembling a crane's beak, about an inch long, that explosively split open when ripe with a satisfying 'pop'

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat, rounded clumps 1-2 feet tall and wide, with multiple stems arising from a central crown

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Upright stems with a slightly sticky, hairy texture that may leave a faint green residue on your fingers

habitat: Extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation, likely an escape from cultivation near gardens or old homesteads. When found, it would prefer partially shaded woodland edges, moist meadows, or disturbed areas with rich, well-drained soil.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as deeply divided rosettes, soft green and fuzzy to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with pink to purple flowers opening in succession, followed by the distinctive crane's-bill seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open explosively, while leaves may develop reddish tints before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only the crown and root system dormant underground.

funFact: The seed pods of crane's-bills are like tiny natural catapults - when ripe, they explosively split and fling seeds up to 25 feet away, complete with an audible 'pop' that you can actually hear in a quiet garden!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with wild geranium, our common native crane's-bill, but wood crane's-bill has more deeply divided leaves and typically shows more prominent dark veining in its petals. Remember: wood crane's-bill has more 'cuts' in its leaves, like intricate woodland lacework.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these true geraniums with the common garden 'geraniums' sold at nurseries - those are actually pelargoniums from South Africa! True geraniums like this one are hardy perennials that can survive New England winters, while pelargoniums are tender and need to be brought indoors.
compareHints: Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining. Unlike the weedy Herb Robert, it lacks the strong musky odor and forms neat garden-worthy clumps rather than sprawling everywhere. It's much rarer than meadow crane's-bill and prefers shadier woodland conditions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
